Let <MATH_0001> be a scheme.
Let <MATH_0002> be an algebraic space over <MATH_0003>.
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> If <MATH_0004> is an isomorphism then <MATH_0005>
is an fpqc covering of <MATH_0006>.
<STRUCT_0003> If <MATH_0007> is an fpqc covering and for each
<MATH_0008> we have an fpqc covering <MATH_0009>, then
<MATH_0010> is an fpqc covering.
<STRUCT_0004> If <MATH_0011> is an fpqc covering
and <MATH_0012> is a morphism of algebraic spaces then
<MATH_0013> is an fpqc covering.
<STRUCT_0005>

Part (1) is clear. Consider <MATH_0001> and
<MATH_0002> an fpqc covering as in (3). By
Morphisms of Spaces, Lemma <REF_0001>
the morphisms <MATH_0003>
are flat. If <MATH_0004> is a morphism from an affine scheme
towards <MATH_0005>, then set <MATH_0006>. The assumption
on <MATH_0007> means there exists a standard fpqc covering
<MATH_0008> and morphisms <MATH_0009> covering
<MATH_0010> for certain <MATH_0011>. By the universal property of the fibre product
we obtain morphisms <MATH_0012> over <MATH_0013> also.
Hence <MATH_0014> is an fpqc covering.
This proves (3).

<STRUCT_0001><STRUCT_0002>
Let <MATH_0015> and <MATH_0016> be as
in (2). Let <MATH_0017> be a morphism from an affine scheme towards <MATH_0018>.
By assumption there exists a standard fpqc covering
<MATH_0019> and morphisms <MATH_0020>
covering <MATH_0021> for some indices <MATH_0022>. By assumption there exist
standard fpqc coverings
<MATH_0023>
and morphisms <MATH_0024> covering
<MATH_0025> for some indices <MATH_0026>. By
Topologies, Lemma <REF_0002>
the family <MATH_0027> is a standard fpqc covering.
Hence we conclude that <MATH_0028>
is an fpqc covering.
